note: Purananuru 56.3-6 sets out the conch-white plough-bearer with the palmyra banner and the gem-dark one with the bird banner as two of four separate gods; Paripadal 1.3-11 gives the same emblems (வால் வளை மேனி, நாஞ்சில், சேவல் அம் கொடி) to one god addressed in the singular.
teaches: Held together, the pair shows that the emblem sets of Balarama and Thirumal were fixed common iconography, but that the Paripadal's Vaishnava singer had already fused the two brothers into one object of worship that the puram poet still counted as two gods.

note: Paripadal 1.32-33 says Thirumal's coming is hard to know even for sages free of confusion; Tirumanthiram 13 puts Vishnu who measured the earth among the gods who, measuring by thought, still cannot conceive the Lord. On the plain reading the two give the unknowable highest place to different gods, and one puts the other's god among the baffled seekers.
teaches: The same argument from unknowability served two rival theologies, and the Saiva poet reuses it by moving Thirumal from the place of the unknown into the place of the seeker, so ineffability became a way to rank gods.

note: Purananuru 59 tells the Pandya he is like the sun to his foes and like the moon to us (ஞாயிறு அனையை ... திங்கள் அனையை); Paripadal 1.41-45 tells the god he is grace to those who love him and terror to foes, the moon and the burning sun, with no marker of likeness.
teaches: The devotional poet took the king-praise formula of grace to friends and fire to foes and dropped its marker of comparison, so what the court poet offers as a simile becomes in the hymn a statement of identity.
audit_text_issue: Paripadal 1 lines 46-47 (ஐந் தலை, மடங்கல்) are of uncertain reference.

note: Purananuru 56 makes the Pandya equal (ஒத்தீயே) to each of four gods in one quality; Paripadal 1.53-57 says no one can be found of whom to say the god is like them, so he is like only himself (நின்னோர் அனையை); both describe the bird-bannered god's body with the same formula, மண்ணுறு மணி (Pura 56.5, Pari 1.62).
teaches: The pairing shows a limit to the பூவைநிலை way of praising a king by the gods: the likeness runs one way only, since a king can be measured by a god but the hymn finds nothing by which to measure the god.

note: Kural 7 says only those who reach the feet of the one without comparison (தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான்) are freed from the mind's care; Paripadal 1.53-68 finds no likeness for the god (நின்னோர் அனையை) and ends with hearts made secure (ஏமுறு நெஞ்சத்தேம்) worshipping the shade of his feet.
teaches: The couplet's two terms, the incomparable one and refuge at his feet, appear in the hymn as a sequence: the singer first tries and fails to find a simile, and only then turns to the feet, so the Kural's maxim reads as the summary of a hymn's movement.

note: Paripadal 2.5-12 tells the ages of the world in the order sky (as sound), wind, fire, water, earth; Thiruppugazh 21 names Mayon as the one who became sky, wind, fire, water and earth in the same order, and the seven worlds, yet touches none of them.
teaches: The five-element order credited to Thirumal survives a thousand years into Arunagirinathar, but what the Sangam singer told as successive ages of the world's making the later poet states as the god's present pervasion of all things.

note: Tirumanthiram 7 declares the Lord elder to the three (மூவர்க்கும் மூத்தவன்) and father to the one who calls him father; Paripadal 2.20-23 makes Thirumal younger to those who call him younger than the conch-white brother and elder to those who call him elder.
teaches: Both poets let the god become the kin-name the worshipper uses, but only the Paripadal applies the rule to seniority itself, so where Tirumular fixes his Lord as eldest the earlier hymn shows rank among gods as a matter of the believer's tradition.

note: Paripadal 1.1-5 addresses Thirumal with Balarama's emblems as one god (ஒரு குழை ஒருவனை); Paripadal 2.20-23 names the conch-white palmyra-banner brother as a second figure and leaves open whether Thirumal is his younger or his elder.
teaches: Read together, the two hymns show that the fusion of the brothers in the first song was a devotional claim made against a known two-brother story, which the second song keeps in view by refusing to settle their order.

note: Kural 1 takes the letter அ, first of all letters, as the figure of the First Lord who is first of the world; Paripadal 2.58-59 uses the pointing letters அ, உ and எ (அவ்வும், உவ்வும், எவ்வயினோயும்) to say the god is that, this and whatever place.
teaches: Two early poets built theology from the Tamil alphabet in different ways: the Kural uses the order of the letters to make God the origin, while the hymn uses the pointing letters to make God every possible referent, origin set beside pervasion.

note: Paripadal 2.62-65 counts the seizing of the goat in the sacrifice and the fire oblation as the god's own food; Kural 259 says not to take one creature's life and eat it is better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices. On the plain reading the hymn honours the animal sacrifice that the couplet ranks below abstention.
teaches: The hymn's aside that others will not accept the brahmins' rite (பிறர் உடம்படுவாரா) and the Kural's ranking of not killing over sacrifice show the same quarrel from both sides, so the dispute over animal sacrifice was live within the Tamil tradition itself.

note: Paripadal 2.16-17 names one age of creation after the boar form (கேழல் திகழ்வரக் கோலமொடு பெயரிய ஊழி); Paripadal 3.21-24 tells the deed itself, the god as a boar ploughing up the great earth with his tusk when fire, death and the sun gathered in the sea at the age's end.
teaches: Read together, the two hymns show the boar descent known in Sangam Vaishnava worship both as a label for a cosmic age and as a narrated rescue of the earth from the flood, so the avatar was already a deed that also served to count time.

note: Paripadal 1.32-39 says even sages free of delusion find the god hard to know and asks him to accept inadequate praise; Paripadal 3.45-47 asks whether anyone but the god himself could know what is like him (நின்னைப் புரை நினைப்பின் நீ அலது உணர்தியோ).
teaches: The first hymn stops at the limit of the praiser's knowledge, while the third turns that limit into a claim about the god, that he is the only knower of himself, so the pair shows the apology of the Tamil hymn hardening into a doctrine of self-knowledge.

note: Kural 4 names God as the one without liking or aversion (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்); Paripadal 3.53-58 makes Maal first of the immortals and first also of the asuras who fled from him into the sea, and asks whether there is any 'these are enemies, these friends' for those who know his nature.
teaches: The Kural states the god's freedom from liking and aversion as a bare attribute, while the hymn tests it against the war of gods and demons, where the god plainly took a side, and saves it by making him lord of both, so the pair shows the attribute had to be defended against a mythology of partisan war.

note: Purananuru 35.14-21 tells Killivalavan that his sky-touching umbrella is not to keep off the sun but to shelter suffering subjects, under a sceptre like aram itself; Paripadal 3.74-76 says the god, with grace as umbrella and aram as sceptre, made the twenty-one worlds a single shade with no second shade.
teaches: The puram poet has to argue the king into reading his umbrella as protection, a meaning the king may fail, whereas the hymn makes protection the umbrella's very substance in the god and takes over the royal boast of one shade with no rival, so the pair shows divine kingship and the counsel to kings using one ideal to measure each other.

note: Paripadal 3.63 says 'you are the fragrance in the flower' (பூவினுள் நாற்றம் நீ) in a run of identities; Tirumanthiram 2639 says the Lord is like the fragrance in the flower, the ghee in milk and the juice in fruit (பூவினுள் நாற்றமும் போலுளன்), mingled everywhere.
teaches: The same image of fragrance in the flower is an identity in the Sangam hymn, where the god is the essence of each thing, and a simile in Tirumular, where the Lord is like that essence and stands mingled in things, so the pair shows the later Saiva poet keeping the image while holding the god at one remove from the world he pervades.

note: Tirumanthiram 10 says he himself is the earth, the sky, the fire, the sun, the moon, the rain and the sea (தானே opening each line); Paripadal 4.25-34 says only that two of the god's qualities are in each of the sun, moon, rain, earth, flower, water, sky and wind, and that these came about by parting from him (நிற் பிரிந்து).
teaches: The two lists cover nearly the same things, but the Sangam hymn keeps the god outside them, each element holding a pair of his qualities as a share that left him, while Tirumular erases the gap and makes him the things themselves, so the pair shows identity with the elements was a later and stronger claim than participation.

note: Paripadal 1.40-51 says you are the moon, the sun, the sky and the earth; Paripadal 4.25-32 says your coolness is in the moon, your heat in the sun, your form and sound in the sky.
teaches: Inside one collection the god is first said to be the moon and the sun and then said to have only lent them his qualities, so the anthology holds both the identity form and the participation form of praise without choosing between them.

note: Purananuru 56.1-8 gives four gods four banners: the bull, the palm (பனைக்கொடி) of the conch-white one with the plough, the bird of the sapphire-dark one, the peacock; Paripadal 4.37-41 gives the dark god the bird, the palm, the plough and the elephant, and says there is no banner that is not his. On the plain reading the palm banner belongs to a different god in one poem and to Mal in the other.
teaches: The puram poet needs four separate gods so that the king can match each in one excellence, while the devotional poet folds the elder brother's palm and plough into Mal's own emblems, so the pair shows how a hymn's claim of sole lordship rearranged the very iconography the court poets used as a fixed set.

note: Paripadal 4.11-21 tells of பிருங்கலாதன் tormented by his father, the god embracing the son and tearing the father's chest with his claws from the broken pillar (ஒடி தூண்); Thiruppugazh 870 tells of a child chanting நம நாராயணாய, the father asking where his god is, and the lion bursting from the pillar to tear Hiranya's chest.
teaches: In the Sangam hymn the story turns on the god's two acts on two chests, the embrace and the tearing, while Arunagirinathar's version turns on the child's recitation of the name and the father's challenge, so the pair shows the Prahlada story shifting its centre from the god's protecting hand to the power of the uttered name.

note: Kural 4 names God as the one without liking or aversion (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்); Paripadal 4.49-55 says the god has harm and grace, cruelty and rightness wherever these are found and none where they are not, and treats the lives of those who praise him and those who do not without exchange, having neither foes nor kin.
teaches: The Kural defines the god by what he lacks, while the hymn shows what that lack allows: he can hold cruelty and grace alike because they answer what is in things rather than his own preference, so freedom from liking and aversion is seen to include, not exclude, the god's harshness.

note: Tirumanthiram 3021 asks where he is and answers that the Lord stands everywhere like rain; Paripadal 4.65-70 names the banyan, the kadamba, the river islet and the trackless hill, where he dwells under a different name in each, and concludes எவ் வயினோயும் நீயே, you are the one in every place.
teaches: Tirumular reaches omnipresence through the image of rain falling on all places alike, while the Sangam poet reaches it by gathering particular shrines with their own local names, so the pair shows the claim 'he is everywhere' first serving to unite many local cults under one god before it became a claim about space.

note: Paripadal 2.20-23 says the god is younger to those who call him younger and elder to those who call him elder; Paripadal 4.69-73 says he bears a different name in each place, sits in the folded hands of his devotees and is the servant (ஏவலாளன்) of each of them.
teaches: The rule that the god takes the place each believer gives him begins in Paripadal 2 as a way out of a dispute over rank, and in Paripadal 4 it is extended to names, places and finally to service, so the pair shows accommodation growing from a theological truce into the god's subordinating himself to every worshipper.

note: Paripadal 5.1-4 (பனிக் கடல் ... புக்கு ... சூர் மா முதல் தடிந்து) and Thirumurugatruppadai 45-46 and 60 (பனிக்கடல் கலங்கவுள் புக்குச் சூர்முதல் தடிந்த ... மாமுதல் தடிந்த) tell the Sur deed in nearly the same words.
teaches: The near-identical phrasing in two different collections shows the Sur killing already had a fixed verbal formula, a shared stock of Murugan praise that both poets drew on rather than one poem borrowing a picture from the other.

note: Akananuru 242 calls the velan who holds the veri rite ignorant (அறியா வேலன்): he blames the god for what is love; Paripadal 5.15-17 says the velan's praise and veri are neither true nor false, since the world lies within the god's bound.
teaches: Read together, the pair shows that the akam mockery of the velan was not a rejection of Murugan: the devotional poet keeps the rite valid at the level of the god while conceding that its particular verdicts may miss, which is exactly the room the akam friend exploits.

note: Paripadal 5.9 names the split hill only by its crane name (குருகொடு பெயர் பெற்ற மால் வரை); Thiruppugazh 38 names it க்ரவுஞ்சம் and has it split together with the drying of the sea.
teaches: The Sangam poet renders the Sanskrit name Krauncha by its Tamil meaning, a hill named with the crane, while Arunagirinathar uses the Sanskrit name outright, so the pair shows the same deed passing from a translated to a borrowed name across a thousand years.

note: Purananuru 55.1-2 (மலைப் பெருவில் பாம்புஞாண் ... ஒரு கணை ... மூவெயில்) and Paripadal 5.24-25 (நாகம் நாணா, மலை வில்லாக, மூவகை ஆர் எயில் ஓர் அழல்-அம்பின்) give the three-forts deed in the same parts: mountain bow, serpent string, one arrow; both also turn on Siva's forehead eye.
teaches: The same tripura formula serves a puram poet as the vehicle of counsel to a Pandya king and a devotional poet as the prelude to Murugan's birth, showing that Siva's deed was common stock usable for statecraft and worship alike in the Sangam period.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 151-154 shows Siva only as one of three lords who come to see Murugan, with Uma, three unwinking eyes and the three forts destroyed; Paripadal 5.22-47 tells how that same god's union with Uma led to Murugan's birth.
teaches: The guide poem gives the kinship only as epithets (son of the god of the banyan, line 256) and shows Siva as a visiting lord, while the Paripadal narrates the birth in full, so the pair shows the story was known to both but told only where a poem chose to narrate rather than to direct a pilgrim.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 253-255 (நெடும்பெருஞ் சிமையத்து நீலப் பைஞ்சுனை ... அறுவர் பயந்த) and Paripadal 5.48-49 (இமயத்து நீலப் பைஞ் சுனைப் பயந்தோர்) set the birth in the same blue pool and give him six mothers.
teaches: Both poems use நீலப் பைஞ்சுனை and the six who bore him, but only the Paripadal says who the six were and why their chastity stayed whole, so the guide poem's single epithet is seen to presuppose a full birth story its hearers already knew.

note: Paripadal 5 has six of the seven sages' wives bear him; Thiruppugazh 372 names him the six-faced one who drank at the breasts of the six (அறுவர் முலையுணு).
teaches: In the Paripadal the six are mothers by conception through the fire, while in the Thiruppugazh they have become nurses he drank from, so the pair shows the six mothers' role shifting from bearing to nursing as the Krittika story settled.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai ends with the god giving the suppliant a rare gift (பெறலரும் பரிசில்) that makes him stand alone in the world; Paripadal 5.79-81 says we ask not wealth, gold or pleasure but grace, love and aram.
teaches: The guide poem frames devotion in the bard's economy of gifts, while the Paripadal explicitly refuses material gifts, so the pair shows two Sangam answers to what one should ask of Murugan, the patron's reward and the ethical state.

note: Kural 241 ranks the wealth of அருள் above the wealth of goods, which even the base possess; Paripadal 5.80-81 refuses பொருளும் பொன்னும் and asks அருளும் அன்பும் அறனும்.
teaches: The Kural makes the ranking a general maxim about kinds of wealth, and the Paripadal turns that same ranking into the content of a prayer, showing the ethical scale used as the measure of what to ask a god for.
audit_text_issue: Paripadal 5 line 78 differs strongly from another edition.

note: Paripadal 5 asks Murugan for love (அன்பும்) instead of wealth; Thiruppugazh 986 asks for love growing ever greater, with tears, melting and faltering speech, and only then for the stainless meaning.
teaches: The Sangam prayer names love as one of three ethical gifts, while the Thiruppugazh makes love itself the whole request and describes its bodily signs, so the pair traces anbu changing from a virtue asked for into the felt experience of bhakti.

note: Kural 18 says that if the sky dries, festival and worship cease even for the gods; Paripadal 6.1-13 shows the rain that has come ending in incense, flowers, oblation and fire (புகை, பூ, அவி ஆராதனை, அழல்) at the river's arrival.
teaches: The Kural argues from absence that worship hangs on rain, and the Paripadal shows the positive side as one continuous scene from sea to cloud to river to offering, adding what the couplet leaves out: the same flood that feeds the rite also brings lovers together, so festival here means love as much as worship.

note: Kural 1251 has desire's axe break the door of restraint (நிறை); Paripadal 6.22-23 has the flood break its dam as lovers of one desire break the restraint that fills the heart (உளம் நிறை உடைத்தென).
teaches: The Kural's woman speaks of restraint broken as her private defeat, while the Paripadal makes the same breaking of நிறை the measure of a flood the whole town celebrates with drums, so the pair shows the Kural's image of a lost guard was also, in the festival, a public and welcome release.

note: Akananuru 296 makes the husband's bathing in the great Vaigai with a dark girl the gossip of Koodal; Paripadal 6.26-43 shows the whole town, young and old, rich and strong, going down to play in the same river.
teaches: Read against the Paripadal's crowd at the fords, the Akananuru friend's charge cannot be that he bathed in the Vaigai, since everyone did; the scandal lies in whom he bathed with, so the akam reproach depends on a public festival that the akam poem itself never describes.

note: Naladiyar 370 says fresh floodwater and a courtesan's friendship are alike, both ending when their source ends; Paripadal 6.72-75 has the wife say love's shrinking and swelling is the Vaiyai's flood.
teaches: The Naladiyar uses the flood's ebb to condemn bought love and spare the household, but the Paripadal puts the same flood image in the wife's mouth against her own husband, so the didactic contrast of faithful wife and fickle courtesan breaks down once the river festival shows the husband's love rising and falling like the stream.

note: Kural 1134 says love's fierce flood carries off the raft (புணை) of shame and manliness; Paripadal 6.80-81 says the husband's chest, like a log in the river, became a raft (புணை) for women skilled at seizing.
teaches: In the Kural the raft is the lover's own virtue swept away by his desire, in the Paripadal the man himself is the raft that others ride, so the same river figure moves from an inner confession to a wife's accusation, and the festival's real floats show where the Kural's metaphor came from.

note: Naladiyar 222 says those who live by water do not rage when the flood breaks the dam but dam it again, as one bears a valued friend's repeated wrongs; Paripadal 6.83-87 says that even when the breached sluice is closed the spray still wells, as her burning goes on after he returns.
teaches: The two poems use the same breached dam for opposite claims: the Naladiyar makes re-damming the picture of calm forbearance that works, while the Paripadal wife says closing the breach does not stop the leak, so the pair shows that the moralist's patience is exactly what the wronged wife declares impossible.

note: In Akananuru 266 the wife says the husband's water-play with young women in the evening flood is gossip but that what hurts is his oath by Murugan of Alaivay; in Paripadal 6.88-96 the husband, accused after the water-play, swears by cool Parankunram.
teaches: Both husbands answer a water-play charge with an oath to a Murugan shrine, but the Akananuru wife treats the oath as the worse betrayal while the Paripadal lets the oath pass into a reconciliation brokered by others, so the pair shows the festival hymn softening into play what the akam anthology records as a wound.

note: In Kural 1313 the man complains that whatever garland he wears she says he wore it for another woman; in Paripadal 6.91-92 the wife asks who pressed into his garland and what touched it, and he blames the river.
teaches: The Kural states the suspicious garland as a pure case of love's jealousy, with no cause given, while the Paripadal gives the garland a real crushing and a real crowd in the water, so the pair shows the couplet's general complaint distilled from a festival in which the evidence truly could point either way.

note: Kural 1302, spoken by the friend, says sulking is like salt and a little too much spoils it; Paripadal 6.98-99 has those around the wife say that if the sulk festers much love is spoiled (துனி நனி கன்றிடின் காமம் கெடூஉம்).
teaches: The same counsel to a sulking wife appears in both, but the Paripadal shows it said aloud at the festival and then acted on by skilled pleaders until the sulk is understood, so the Kural's measure of salt turns out to belong to a social practice of reconciliation, not only to one friend's private advice.

note: Kural 17 says even the wide sea would lose its nature if the cloud that drew from it gave nothing back; Paripadal 7.1-10 begins with clouds that have drawn the dark sea fully (பௌவம் செவ்விதா அற முகந்து) and ends the sentence with the land's good and beauty swelling as the Vaiyai comes.
teaches: The couplet states the exchange between sea and cloud as a warning about withholding, while the song follows the same water through rain, falls and river into the Pandya fields, so together they show that the Kural's abstract cycle was the felt shape of the flood festival, praised in the hymn as the return the couplet only demands.

note: Ainkurunuru 69 has the wife say she has seen the husband's woman crying, eyes reddened, when the cool flood with its flowers swept her sand-play away at the crowded ford; Paripadal 7.25-26 lists among the town's cries the young women weeping that the flood broke the dolls they drew in the sand.
teaches: In the hymn the weeping over sand dolls is one anonymous cry among many on flood day, while the akam wife picks out one such girl to mock as her husband's new woman, so the pair shows the akam poet taking a stock festival scene and turning it into a mark of the rival's childishness.

note: Akananuru 266 has the wife tell her husband that his bathing yesterday in the new flood with young women, gazing again and again at one woman's rain-cool eyes, is now loud gossip; Paripadal 7.65-76 shows the scene itself: a bard praises a bather's eyes, the lover who looked at the bathers is pulled into the mud and his head trodden on by the woman in her sulk.
teaches: The Akananuru gives only the aftermath, the wife's reproach once talk has spread, whereas the Paripadal shows the gazing at the eyes and the quarrel breaking out at once in the river, so together they show the river bathing as the very occasion of the marutham sulk, with its offence and its punishment both public.

note: Kural 1311 has the woman refuse her lover's chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; in Paripadal 7.69-75 the woman's fury falls on her lover because he looked at the ornaments of the bathing women (யாறு ஆடு மேனி அணி கண்ட).
teaches: The couplet makes the man's being looked at enough for oodal, the hymn makes his looking the offence, and the song's crowded bathing shows why both could be true at once: in the festival everyone sees and is seen, so the sulk needs no act of straying, only the eyes.

note: Naladiyar 370 makes the fresh flood (புதுப்புனல்) a type of what does not last: it ends when the rain ends; Paripadal 7.84-86 prays to the Vaiyai's flood that the bathing in it may never be left (நின் படிந்து நீங்காமை).
teaches: The same new flood that the ethical quatrain uses to prove that pleasures and loves dry up is, in the festival hymn, the object of a prayer for permanence, so the pair shows the didactic poet reversing the devotional value of the river by fixing on its ending rather than its yearly return.

note: In Akananuru 166 the husband soothes his wife by calling on the Velur god to afflict him if he went to the other woman, and the other woman exposes the lie; in Paripadal 8.65-66 the wife forbids such an oath by Murugan, since the god's true spear would eat him.
teaches: The Akananuru shows the god-oath used lightly as a husband's comfort, the Paripadal shows a wife who takes the same self-curse seriously enough to block it, so together they reveal that the oath was believed to bind the swearer bodily and that a knowing wife could protect a lying husband from it.

teaches: On the plain reading of each, the two poems disagree on whom a broken god-witnessed oath strikes, the deceived women in the Kuruntokai and the perjurer in the Paripadal, so the pair shows two Sangam answers to where the god's punishment falls.

note: Paripadal 8.96-108 shows the crowd at Parankundram carrying flowers, incense and lamps and asking for children, wealth and victory; Thiruppugazh 8, sung at Parangiri, confesses that the poet never worshipped with flowers or walked round the hill and asks only that Murugan come at the hour of death.
teaches: The rites the Sangam festival performs as means to this-world ends become, at the same hill a thousand years later, the list of duties the devotee confesses he failed, and the request moves from children and wealth to rescue at death.

note: Kural 17 says even the great sea loses its nature if the cloud withholds rain; Paripadal 8.128-130 prays that the hill's streaming falls and springs last even when the sky dries and the earth cracks (மண் பரிய வானம் வறப்பினும், மன்னுகமா).
teaches: The Kural makes every water, the sea included, depend on rain, and the Paripadal asks that the god's waterfall be exempt from that law, which is what marks the shrine's water as sacred rather than natural.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 6 names the god only as husband of a bright-browed woman of spotless chastity (மறுவில் கற்பின் வாணுதற் கணவன்); Paripadal 9.8-11 names her as the daughter of the thousand-eyed one and sets the wedding at Parankunram, marked by rain in summer.
teaches: Held together, the guide poem's opening epithet turns out to rest on a wedding story that the Paripadal ties to one hill, which explains why Parankunram, the hill of that marriage, is the first abode the guide poem then visits.

note: Kural 1330 says sulking is love's pleasure and its pleasure is the embrace that follows; Paripadal 9.12-22 ranks love, equal union and karpu, and places the courtesan, the reproach and the சுணங்கறை inside karpu, with their fruit in the sulk (ஊடல்).
teaches: The Kural gives the sulk's worth as a man's two-line saying, while the Paripadal builds it into a ranked theory addressed to Vedic scholars and then uses it to excuse a god's wives, so the pair shows oodal already held as doctrine of Tamil porul, citable to outsiders and to the gods.

note: In both a wife refuses the husband who has been with other women: Kural 1311 says 'I will not come near your chest, philanderer' (நண்ணேன் பரத்தநின் மார்பு); in Paripadal 9.30-40 the wife blesses him ironically and cries 'don't come near' (குறுகல்), while the rival gives him her chest (மார்பு அளிப்பாளை).
teaches: The Kural's refusal is private and the rival only imagined, while the Paripadal stages the same refusal with the rival present and offering the very chest the wife denies, so the pair shows the one gesture of refusing the chest working as a quarrel between two women, not only between wife and husband.

note: Thiruppugazh 12, a Parankunram song, has Indra's daughter and the hunter girl both embrace Murugan's twelve shoulders; Paripadal 9 sets the same two wives at the same hill in a quarrel with blows of garlands.
teaches: The later hymn keeps the two consorts side by side in a single embrace, while the Sangam song lets them fight over him at the same shrine, which shows the co-wives' rivalry was once part of the hill's sacred lore and was smoothed away as the pair became fixed icons of devotion.

note: Thiruppugazh 18 names Murugan of south Parankunram as the one who took the girl the hill people gave (குன்றவர்கள் தந்தபெண்); Paripadal 9.67-69 has Valli's kin, the kurinji hill-men (குறிஞ்சிக் குன்றவர் ... வள்ளி தமர்), turn the wives' quarrel into a thumbai battle on that hill.
teaches: In the hymn the hill people appear only as givers of the bride, while in the Paripadal they stay her partisans after the marriage and fight for her against the sky-born wife, so the pair shows Valli's marriage remembered as an alliance with her kin that carried on into the god's household.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 101-102 gives one of the six faces to smiling with Valli, the hill-dwellers' daughter, after its opening epithet for the chaste wife; Paripadal 9.81 names the god as lord of the bond of love along the path of the bond of karpu (கற்பு இணை நெறியூடு அற்பு இணைக் கிழமை).
teaches: The guide poem lists the two marriages separately, one as an epithet and one as a face's work, while the Paripadal joins them in one phrase after teaching the order of love, so the pair shows the two consorts being read as the two branches of akam, karpu and the love of free choice, united in one god.

note: Akananuru 296's friend turns the hero away because he bathed in the great Vaigai with the dark girl (பெருநீர் வையை அவளொடு ஆடி) and the talk is like Koodal's clamour; Paripadal 10.19-23 lists chaste wives and courtesans (பதிவத மாதர், பரத்தையர்) going together to the Vaigai at Koodal.
teaches: Since the festival put wives and courtesans in the same flood openly, the friend's charge in Akananuru 296 cannot be the bathing itself, a licensed public pleasure, but the companion he chose, so the akam poem turns a shared civic rite into private evidence.

note: Kuruntokai 37's tusker strips yaa branches to ease his mate's hunger, left for the heroine to read as the hero's love; Paripadal 10.42-52 has a tusker turn back to embrace his terrified mate and says outright சிறந்தார் நடுக்கம் சிறந்தார் களையல்.
teaches: The Paripadal poet spells out in one line the sense that Kuruntokai 37 leaves implied, which shows that the caring elephant pair was read by the poets themselves as an image of the lover who removes the beloved's distress.

note: Kural 1145 says love grows sweeter each time it is exposed, as drinking is craved each time one is drunk; Paripadal 10.63-68 likens lovers who hide their love from gossip to drinkers who hide their drunkenness.
teaches: Both join love and toddy, but the Kural's lover welcomes exposure while the Paripadal's festival lovers hide from it, so the same comparison serves to praise and to fear gossip, and the couplet's bravado reads as one stance among those the poets knew.

note: Akananuru 266's wife says her husband played in the evening flood with young women and lost his shame (நாண்இழந்து), and the talk is loud as a feast; Paripadal 10.63-68 shows lovers in the flood hiding their joy for fear of gossip (அலர் அஞ்சி).
teaches: The Paripadal shows that the flood-play crowd expected lovers to hide, so the wife's charge that he 'lost his shame' accuses him of breaking a restraint the festival itself kept, not of joining the play.

note: Kural 1066 says nothing degrades the tongue more than asking, even water for a cow; Paripadal 10.87-88 has bathers who, seeing what they lack, do good works in hope before they speak the shame of asking (இளிவரவு கூறாமுன்).
teaches: The festival bathers apply the Kural's horror of asking even to what they want from the river, choosing an offering over a spoken request, so the ethic against begging shaped how people framed a petition in worship.

note: Kural 211 measures giving without return by the rain, to which the world gives nothing back; Paripadal 10.125-127 measures the Vaigai's flood over the fields by the Vazhuthi who pours gold into poets' hands.
teaches: The Kural makes nature the model for the giver, while the Paripadal makes the king the model for nature, so the pair shows the comparison between rain and royal giving could run in both directions, with the Pandya's gift treated as the surer standard.

teaches: What the puram poet urges on a Vazhuthi as a duty to be kept, the devotional poet takes as so settled a fact of the Pandya house that it can serve as the vehicle for praising the river itself.

note: Paripadal 11.37-38 asks who notices the days run down (நாள் குறைபடுதல் காணுநர் யாரே) as the flood wanes like the moon; Kural 334 says the day is a saw cutting life, for those who can perceive it (உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்).
teaches: Both turn on the same observation, that daily loss goes unseen, but the Paripadal draws from it a request to the river to slow down and keep its plenty, while the Kural draws a warning to the perceptive; the image of unnoticed waning could serve plenty as well as renunciation.

note: Natrinai 80 names in one line a girl who bathes in the cold pond of the month of Thai with her jewelled companions (தைஇத் திங்கள் தண் கயம் படியும்); Paripadal 11.74-92 sets out the rite itself: Aathirai, the brahmins, the elder women of the ford, the dawn bath and the fire.

note: In Paripadal 11.80 unmarried girls bathe under the brahmins' fire rite praying 'may the wide land not be scorched'; Kural 55 says it rains at the word of the wife who does not worship a god but worships her husband. On the plain reading these name incompatible sources of the rain women can bring: public worship by maidens, or a wife's devotion that sets worship of a god aside.
teaches: Held together, the pair shows two rival accounts of women's power over the rain, the festival rite of the unmarried at the river and the wife's domestic devotion, and the Kural's தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் reads as a choice of the second over the first.

note: Paripadal 11.106-110 tells literally of a youth whom the Vaigai's current carries off while a girl takes his heart (கடும் புனல் கை வாங்க, நெஞ்சம் அவள் வாங்க); in Kalittokai 98 a husband swears he was delayed bathing in the Vaigai's new flood, and his wife answers that people saw the new flood drag him off, a flood that was a woman.
teaches: The wife's figure of the woman as a flood that carried him off is the Paripadal's festival event turned into an accusation, so the river festival was both the occasion of a man being swept away by a look and the stock excuse for it, and the Kalittokai's irony depends on the audience knowing the Paripadal scene.

note: Paripadal 11.120-121 has the bathing women ask that for seven births, without growing old, their rich kin last and bear children; in Kuruntokai 49 a wife asks her husband that even when this birth gives way to the next he be her husband and she the one close to his heart.
teaches: What the Kuruntokai wife says privately to one man, the Paripadal's women ask together of the river at a public festival, so the wish to keep the same spouse beyond this birth was a recognised petition of the Thai rite, not only one woman's vow of love.

note: Paripadal 11.122-123 has onlookers call a girl a striking goddess (தாக்கு அணங்கு) whose eyes are Kaaman's army (காமன் படை); Kural 1082 has the man say that her returning his look is a striking goddess come with an army (தாக்கணங்கு தானைக்கொண் டன்ன).
teaches: The rare compound and the army come together in both, so the Kural's lover is speaking a festival idiom: what the Paripadal's crowd shouts as a warning to all who see the girl, the Kural turns into one man's private experience of a single returned glance.

note: Kalittokai 67.3-5 says the Vaiyai beating against the wall (மதில் பொரூஉம்) is the only enemy the walled town has known; Paripadal 12.9 has the town hear that the Vaiyai has come beating against Madurai's wall (மதுரை மதில் பொரூஉம்) and rush out in finery to meet it.
teaches: The akam poem turns the river's assault on the wall into a boast that no army ever reached Madurai, and the hymn shows what that only siege was like inside the walls, a summons that sends the whole town to dress and ride out, so together they show the flood as the city's one welcomed attack, the festival standing where war stands for other towns.

note: In Kalittokai 67.6-9 the wife says she will sulk when her husband comes showing the wounds and scars (புண், வடு) that other women's garlands (கோதையால் அலைத்த) left on him, and her heart gives way when she sees him; in Paripadal 12.57-73 the wife herself beats her husband with her garland (கமழ் கோதை கோலாப் புடைத்து), then fears a scar on his chest (வடு அஞ்சி) and her quarrel passes.
teaches: In the Kalittokai the garland-wound is evidence against the husband, written on him by rival women, while in the hymn the wife wields the garland herself and her fear of the scar is what ends her sulk, so the pair shows the garland-blow as a festival game of the Vaiyai town whose meaning, accusation or claim, depends on whose hand struck it.

note: Kural 1321 has the woman say that though he has no fault, his grace has the power to bring on a sulk; in Paripadal 12.55-60 the man has eyed another woman's breasts, and when beaten he 'sees no fault' (பிழை ஒன்றும் காணான்) and bows asking to be told it, and the onlookers call him the pure one (தூயவனைக் காண்மின்).
teaches: The couplet takes the faultless lover of the oodal at the woman's word, while the hymn shows a crowd that has watched him look and mocks his innocence as he begs to hear his fault, so together they show that the faultless husband of the sulk was a convention its audience knew to be a pose, and that the Kural's version is the inside view of a scene the festival saw from outside.

note: Paripadal 7.65-76 has a woman, angry that her lover looked at the bathers, punish him in the river; Paripadal 12.55-74 has the same offence of looking at another woman at the flood and the same sulk, carried through the blow and his fall to her return to his breast, which the poet credits to the Vaiyai's flood (வல்லதால், வையைப் புனல்).
teaches: Song 7 leaves the river quarrel at the lover's punishment, while song 12 carries the same quarrel to its making-up and gives the river the credit, so the two Vaiyai songs show that the oodal episode was told in the hymns in order to praise the flood as the reconciler, the go-between that akam poems give to a friend or a bard.

note: Kalavazhi Narpathu 30 likens the pooled blood of the battlefield, dragging killed elephants, to a flood that rolls boulders down the hill (மலையுருட்டு நீர்போல்); Paripadal 12.84-85 sees the Vaiyai in the morning of the rains red with turbid blood (கலிழ் செங் குருதித்தே) and names it the river of the king whose army kills in war.
teaches: The war poem uses the hill torrent as the image for battle blood and the hymn uses battle blood as the image for the monsoon torrent, so held together they show the comparison running both ways for Tamil poets: the king's killing is a flood and his river's flood is his killing, the river's redness counting as his fame.

note: Kural 1064 says the dignity that will not beg even when nothing is left is too great for all the world to hold (இடமெல்லாம் கொள்ளா); Paripadal 12.101 ends by telling the Vaiyai that this flower-topped world cannot hold its fame (நின் புகழ் கொள்ளாது, இம் மலர் தலை உலகே).
teaches: The same measure, a greatness the world is too small to hold, is given by the hymn to a river's yearly plenty and by the Kural to a destitute man's refusal to ask, so the pair shows the ethical book taking the praise formula of abundance and fixing it on the one thing that has no abundance at all.

note: Both name the same five, taste, light or sight, touch, sound and smell; the Kural, in its chapter on renunciants, puts the world in the grasp of the one who discerns them, while Paripadal 13 says the five and the faculties that take them are the god.
teaches: The Kural's five, which the renunciant must master, are in the Paripadal the god himself, so the same old list of five could ground either a discipline of withdrawal from the senses or a worship through them.

note: Paripadal 13 orders the elements sky, wind, fire, water by how many of the five each is known through; Tirumanthiram 385 tells the same chain as emergence, space, air, then a doubtful கான், water, the five together.
teaches: Because the Paripadal's count puts fire between wind and water, it supports reading the Tirumanthiram's obscure கான் as fire, and shows the creation chain the later Saiva text tells already present in an early Tamil hymn as a theory of how each element is known.

note: Paripadal 2 says Maal is younger to those who call him the white one's younger brother and elder to those who call him elder; Paripadal 13 makes the plough-bearer one of Maal's own three forms.
teaches: Held together, the two hymns show Paripadal poets resolving the kinship of Maal and the plough-bearer in two ways: one makes the order of birth depend on who is speaking, the other dissolves the kinship entirely by making the brother a form of the one god.

note: Kural 5 says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise; Paripadal 13 line 47 says the two deeds are absent where his feet are praised, and gives the god a heart set on a single deed.
teaches: The Paripadal sets the Kural's claim inside a theology: the praisers are free of both deeds because the god himself is beyond the three times and holds to one deed, so the Kural's freedom from karma through praise is grounded in what the praised one is.

note: Two hymns by different poets to different gods, Nallezhuthiyar's to Maal and Kesavanar's to Sevvel, close the same way: the god thought of as mother, worship repeated, and இன்னும் இன்னும் asking for more of it.
teaches: Since the same close serves two poets and both Maal and Murugan, the mother-address and the prayer for more worship belong to a shared Paripadal liturgy, not to one poet's devotion or one god's cult.

note: Paripadal 5 refuses wealth, gold and pleasure and asks the god for grace, love and aram; Paripadal 13 asks for nothing but more of the worship, which it calls the fruit of past penance and names its kaamam.
teaches: Read in sequence the two closes show a step in the hymns' idea of what to ask: from the god's virtues instead of wealth to worship as its own reward, so that by Paripadal 13 the act of praising is both the fruit of tapas and the whole of desire.
audit_text_issue: Pari 5 line 78 differs strongly from another edition (packet flag).

note: In Akananuru 194 the heroine hears the peacock cry in the very rains her lover named for his return and he has not come; in Paripadal 14 the peacock's cry on the god's rainy hill is like the words calling the departed lover 'do not delay, come'.
teaches: The Paripadal's simile only works for a hearer who knows the mullai convention the Akananuru poem dramatises, the rains as the deadline of return, so the devotional poet borrows the heroine's grief as an ornament of the god's hill and makes the peacock say the summons she can only feel.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai describes the twice-born at Eragam in full, never failing in the six duties, keeping the three fires and chanting at the proper hour; Paripadal 14 compresses them to a riddle of counts, இரு பிறப்பு, இரு பெயர், ஒரு பெயர், and says the god delights in their aram.
teaches: The idyll's full portrait supplies what the Paripadal's terse count assumes, so its இரு பிறப்பு is the same இருபிறப்பாளர் the idyll names, and the brahmins' ritual life is shown to be, for both poems, one of the things Murugan is praised for enjoying.

note: Paripadal 13.10-13 says the god's chest holds by right (உரிமை) the heaven of those who worship it; Paripadal 15.15-18 says heaven is hard to climb unless the tulasi-wearer grants it, but is gained easily, by right (உரிமை), at Maalirunkunram.
teaches: The same claim of a worshipper's right to heaven is lodged first in the god's body and then in a hill one can walk to, so the pair shows Thirumal's grace being given a place on the map near Madurai.

note: Paripadal thirattu 12 says those who live in Koodal and Parankunram are the ones truly living, and asks who would go to the world of the gods; Paripadal 15.15-18 keeps heaven as the goal and praises Maalirunkunram as the easy way to it.
teaches: One Madurai poet makes the sacred hill a substitute that makes heaven unwanted and another makes it a means to heaven, so the shrine hills could be praised either as better than the world above or as its gate.

note: Paripadal 1.1-13 describes two forms in turn, the white one with the hooded heads, the curved plough and a single earring, then the dark one with the bird banner; Paripadal 15.54-61 lists the single earring, the ringed plough, the tulasi, conch, discus and bird banner in one run of plurals and worships them as the two of great name.
teaches: Song 1 keeps the brothers' marks apart in two portraits, while song 15 pours them into one litany and addresses the pair, so together they show the Balarama and Krishna emblems hardening into a shared catalogue of one double deity.

note: Paripadal 13.22-36 makes the plough-bearer one of three forms of a single god (மூஉரு ஆகிய தலைபிரி ஒருவனை); Paripadal 15 keeps them as two, different in form but one in deed (வேறு வேறு உருவின் ஒரு தொழில் இருவர்), and bows to the two.
teaches: Against song 13's solution, which absorbs the brother as a form of the one god, song 15 keeps two persons and finds their unity in a single deed, like word and meaning, so the Paripadal holds two theologies of the pair.

note: Kural 4 says those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering anywhere at any time; Paripadal 15.49-53 says the god appears in whatever world and removes suffering when people are troubled, and sends worshippers with their families to his hill.
teaches: The Kural puts the movement on the devotee who reaches the feet, while the hymn puts it on a god who comes into each world and on the pilgrim's journey to one hill, so release from suffering is framed as both an inward arrival and a visit.

note: Kural 18 warns that if the sky dries up, festival and worship will cease here, even for the gods; Paripadal 16.48-55 prays that the sky never refuse, so that the sandal, garlands, smoke and offerings of the river festival never dry and the Vaigai never runs dry.
teaches: The Kural states the dependence of worship on rain as a general warning, and the hymn turns the same dependence into a prayer said at the festival it describes, so the couplet's rule is shown at work in the Vaigai rites.

note: Paripadal 12.81-83 has the settled Vaiyai show heaven's beauty as a reflection in its water; Paripadal 16.32-38 makes the flood itself look like the sky through which the star-flowered heavenly Ganga runs, with the lovers' fallen flowers as its stars.
teaches: One poet finds the sky in the clear river after the flood and another in the flood's floating flowers, so the pair shows the Vaiyai as heaven on earth being made both from stillness and from festival litter.

note: Kural 215 likens the wealth of a wise man who helps the world to the village tank filled with water; Paripadal 16.1-4 likens the banks, worn away as the flood carries off pepper, sandal and curd foam, to the giving of a generous lord.
teaches: The Kural uses full water as the image of a giver's wealth, and the Paripadal uses a giver as the image of water taking from its banks, so the pair shows the river-and-giving figure running both ways, with the Paripadal stressing that giving is a wearing away.

note: Paripadal 8.17-28 has the hill answer back and forth (மாறுமாறு அதிர்ப்ப) with the cloud, the cock, the elephants and the caves, and the bees hum like the lute; Paripadal 17.9-21 sets the bards' lute, flute, drum, dancers and singer side by side with bees, tumbi, falls, creepers and peacock, each answering the other (மாறு எதிர் கோடல்).
teaches: In song 8 the echo contest is among the hill's own things and the lute only a likeness for the bees, while song 17 puts the festival's real musicians into the contest against the hill, so together they show the Parankunram echo becoming a set piece in which worshippers and mountain compete as equals.

note: Paripadal 9.70-85 says that on the god's hill dancers outdo dancers and bards outdo those practised in song, the skilled the skilled; Paripadal 17.9-21 matches each human performer not with another performer but with a thing of the hill doing the same act.
teaches: Song 9 makes the festival a rivalry of like with like among people, and song 17 widens the rival to the bee, the falls and the peacock, so the pair shows that for these poets the god's hill was praised by contest itself, and the strongest praise was to have nature enter the contest.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 67-77 marks the god's dwelling on the hill west of Koodal by the bees that sleep in the lotus and hum round the pool flowers opening like eyes; Paripadal 17.37-38 says that when the swingers leap together on festival day the bees that suck the pool flowers' pollen cannot reach them.
teaches: The guide poem gives the hill west of Koodal at rest, its pool bees the sign of the god's ordinary dwelling, and the hymn uses the same pool bees to measure the festival, when the crowd drives them off, so the pair shows the same place on its common day and on its feast day.

note: Kural 43 makes the chief duty of the householder the care of ancestors, gods, guests, kin and self; Paripadal 17.42-46 says the god's festival and the fine feasting of guests pass in turn between the hill, the Vaiyai and Koodal, and the song closes with a prayer made with kin (யாமும் எம் சுற்றமும்).
teaches: The Kural lays the duties to god, guest and kin on one household, while the hymn shows the same duties carried by a whole region in turn, hill, river and city, so the pair shows the couplet's private order also lived as the civic round of Madurai's festivals.

note: Paripadal 8.10-11 says that because of the god Parankunram equals the Himalaya (பரங்குன்று இமயக் குன்றம் நிகர்க்கும்); Paripadal 18.5-6 says this hill takes up the contest to stand level with the hill that bears the god's glory (ஏறுமாறு ஏற்கும் இக் குன்று).
teaches: Song 8 states the equality as a settled fact granted by the god's presence, and song 18 turns it into a challenge the hill still accepts, so read together they show the Paripadal poets making Parankunram's rank against the northern mountain a standing claim each hymn renews.

note: Kural 1320 has the man say that even when he looks at her thinking, she flares up: whom were you thinking of as you looked? In Paripadal 18.8-14 the woman sees him gaze at a peacock and think, says she knows his thought and demands it, and he answers that he was thinking how the peacock had stolen her bearing.
teaches: The couplet ends on the woman's suspicion with no reply, while the hymn supplies the reply that disarms it, that the thought was of her through the bird that took her grace, so the pair shows the silent gaze as a fixed cause of sulking and the lover's answer as part of the same convention.

note: Kalittokai 95 has the husband say he only watched a quail fight (குறும்பூழ் போர்), and the wife turns each kind of quail fight into a figure for his affairs; in Paripadal 18.12-14 the man says he looked at the peacock and at a quail dazed with revelry, and the woman looked at him as a stranger.
teaches: In the Kalittokai the man's watching of birds is an alibi that the wife exposes, while in the Paripadal his gaze at birds is a lover's thought of her that he can explain away, so the pair shows the same excuse of bird-watching used once for a lie caught and once for a sulk mended on the god's hill.

note: Ainkurunuru 47 has the woman tell the man that her companions know he tells many lies, just like his bard; Paripadal 18.16-22 shows her making the bard see the nail marks, the embrace and the ornaments on the man and calling his song a bloom of lies (பொய் வளம் பூத்தன).
teaches: The Ainkurunuru gives the charge that the bard lies as his master does, and the hymn gives the proof shown to the bard's face, the marks the hill's women left, so together they show the god's festival hill as one of the places where marutham's straying was caught, with the bard's song refuted by the body.

note: Kuruntokai 1 says the hill of the Red One, who killed the demons till the field ran red, is thick with kanthal clusters the colour of blood (குருதிப் பூவின் குலைக்காந் தட்டே); Paripadal 18.35-36 says the close-packed kanthal of the god's hill are like the hands of men defeated in war and bound.
teaches: Both poets make the kanthal of Murugan's hill a sign of his war, but the Kuruntokai reads it by colour, the blood of the slain, and the Paripadal by shape, the clasped hands of the captured, so the pair shows the flower fixed as the god's war emblem while each poet chose a different basis for it.

note: Paripadal 9.8-11 says that when the god married the fawn-like girl, the eyes of the daughter of the thousand-eyed one rained like rain in summer at Parankunram; Paripadal 19.5-7 says the wedding with the peacock-like bride at the same hill seems to vie with that of the bride from heaven.
teaches: In song 9 the second marriage is a wound to the first wife, while song 19 turns the same two weddings into a contest of splendour in which the earthly bride matches the heavenly one, so the hill's lore of two marriages could be sung either as a domestic grief or as the claim that Parankunram brings heaven's festival down to earth.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 71-77 places the god's hill west of Koodal of crowded mansion streets, among wide muddy fields of lotus and bees; Paripadal 19.8-18 fills the whole stretch between the hill and Koodal (குன்றொடு கூடல் இடையெல்லாம்) with a pre-dawn procession of riders, chariots and garlanded heads.
teaches: The guide poem gives the pilgrim the hill's place relative to the city and its quiet fields, and the hymn shows the same stretch on festival day as one continuous human garland, so together they show Parankunram as Madurai's own shrine, whose road from the city was itself part of the festival.
audit_text_issue: Paripadal 19 line 8 may be a dropped heading; line 6 restored by rule.

note: Kural 37 tells us to see the way of aram in the difference between the one who bears the palanquin and the one who rides in it; Paripadal 19.10-13 likens the festival riders on horses and in chariots, in fine ornament and cloth, to those who have done much aram and set out for the world of the excellent to take its fruit.
teaches: Both picture the fruit of aram as riding in finery, but the Paripadal puts that ride in the passage to the next world and uses it only as a simile for festival-goers, while the Kural reads it in this world's ranks, so the pair shows the Kural's hard claim taking a shared image of heavenly reward and pressing it into a judgement on living people.

note: Kural 25 names Indra, lord of the wide heaven, as witness enough to the strength of one who has quenched the five senses; Paripadal 19.50-52 records visitors at the Parankunram painted hall explaining a picture: Indra as the cat, Ahalya, Gautama who had gone out, and her form turned to stone in his anger.
teaches: On the reading that Indra is witness through his own fall, the Kural's single name assumes a story that the Paripadal shows painted on a Madurai temple wall and told aloud to anyone who asked, so the couplet's allusion was not learned lore but a tale ordinary pilgrims were taught from pictures.

note: Paripadal 8.19-21 has the hill's caves (மலை முழை) answer back and forth the cock's crow and the musth elephants' trumpeting that answer the god's elephant and the thunder; Paripadal 19.62-65 has the echoing cave (இசை முழை) take up a lost girl's call and lead her astray.
teaches: In song 8 the cave echo multiplies the god's elephant, his cock and the storm into a sign that the whole hill answers him, while in song 19 the same caves fool a lost girl and the poet calls this the hill's innocent nature, so the pair shows the Parankunram echo used both as a mark of divine presence and as the hill's playful character.

note: In Akananuru 98 the girl fears that if Murugan, the tall Vel smelling of veri, should actually relieve her at the mother's rite, her lover will hear that her pain was something else; Paripadal 19.89-94 says maidens will not reach young men's arms, nor wives their husbands' grace, unless they eat the leftover of the god's elephant at his hill.
teaches: The akam girl's dread makes sense only if Murugan really does rule a girl's union, and the Paripadal states that power openly as a festival rite that maidens and wives perform, so together they show that the akam irony about the veri rite rests on a public belief in the god as the giver of husbands, not on disbelief in him.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 206-217 describes the god as red, in red clothing (செய்யன் சிவந்த ஆடையன்), dancing on every hill with the women's soft shoulders in his arms; Paripadal 19.97-100 tells him his dress and cloak are red, his weapon coral-coloured, his form like fire and his face like the young sun.
teaches: The guide poem's red god is roaming from hill to hill in the kurinji dance, while the hymn addresses the same red figure as the image standing by the kadambu at one shrine, praised by a gathered company, so the pair shows one colour iconography carried from the wandering god of the hill people to the fixed god of a temple.

note: Akananuru 186 has the courtesan say, for the wife's women to overhear, that the wife's real enemy is the husband who leaves women pale and lives in her own house; Paripadal 20.79-82 has the courtesan tell the wife to her face that he is the thief and she is not (அவன் கள்வன்; கள்வி நான் அல்லேன்).
teaches: Together the two show that shifting the blame onto the husband was the courtesan's settled defence in marutham, and that what the Akananuru gives as an overheard boast the festival poem stages as a face-to-face exchange, with the husband's gift on her body as the evidence and a crowd to hear both sides.

note: Kural 913 makes the embrace of women who love for wealth a falsehood, like holding a stranger's corpse in the dark; in Paripadal 20.79-82 the paid woman herself argues that the payment was fair (விலை தந்தான்) and that the falsehood is the man's.
teaches: The Kural judges the bought embrace from the client's side, so the deceit is hers; the Paripadal lets the woman answer from inside the bargain, and on that reading the two cannot both stand, since one places the lie in her love and the other in his gift of what was not his to give.

note: Naladiyar 385 has the wife wonder how women who embrace many chests for gain can do so daily; Paripadal 20.48-51 has the wife's companion call the courtesan a bought woman whose womanhood is common to all (பெண்மைப் பொதுமைப் பிணையிலி).
teaches: The Naladiyar's contrast of chaste wife and common woman is a private wondering, while in the Paripadal the same contrast becomes public abuse at the river, worked out as a farmer's claim on a straying ox, which shows the wife's chastity defended as a household's ownership of the husband and not only as her own shame.

note: Kural 55 says the wife who rises worshipping her husband commands the rain; Paripadal 20.88-89 has onlookers tell a wronged wife that worthy women praise and bow to their husbands even when the husbands slight them (கேள்வரை ஏத்தி இறைஞ்சுவார்).
teaches: The Kural offers the wife's worship of her husband as a source of power over nature, but the Paripadal shows the same ideal used in a quarrel to silence a wife whose husband has given her bangle away, so the couplet's praise of devotion could serve in practice as counsel to put up with a man's straying.

note: Kural 1251 has the woman say desire's axe breaks the door of restraint; Paripadal 20.91-94 has the onlookers say no one can bar men's chests from women and ask whether love stays within its bounds (கட வரை நிற்குமோ காமம்?).
teaches: In the Kural the claim that desire breaks every bound is a woman's confession about her own longing, while in the Paripadal the same claim is turned into an excuse for the husband's straying and urged on the wife, which shows how one maxim about love's force served opposite ends depending on whose desire it named.

note: Kural 1330 says sulking is love's pleasure and its pleasure is the embrace that follows; Paripadal 20.109-112 says it is the Vaiyai's nature to join lovers so that quarrel, friendship, parting, love and toddy are praised together.
teaches: The Kural's rule that the sulk sweetens union is a statement about two lovers, and the Paripadal extends it to a whole town's festival, closing a poem whose centre was a bitter public quarrel by counting that quarrel among the river's pleasures, so the couplet's private economy of oodal is shown working at civic scale.

note: Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet (இறைவன் அடிசேரா தார்) cross the sea of births; Paripadal 21.16 asks only that dwelling at the foot of the god's hill (குன்றத்து அடி உறை) be granted, and line 68 repeats it as dwelling at the god's feet (நின் அடி உறை).
teaches: The Kural's feet are a way out of rebirth, while the Paripadal makes the same feet a place on the ground, the foot of one hill where worshippers ask to go on living, so the pair shows the god's feet as a refuge of release in the ethical book and as a home on earth in the older festival hymn.

note: Kural 1090 says brewed toddy (அடுநறா) delights only those who drink it, unlike love, which delights those who see it; Paripadal 21.20 has a dancer held by the joy of brewed toddy (அடு நறா மகிழ்) sulking at her husband, and the poet says such scenes, when recalled, are a painting's beauty.
teaches: The Kural separates the drinker's private pleasure from the beholder's pleasure in love, while the Paripadal mixes them in one woman, drunk and sulking at her husband, and makes her a picture for onlookers on the hill, so held together they show that at the shrine festival even the drinker's mood became something seen and enjoyed by others.

note: Akananuru 82.1-10 makes the hill country a stage: wind in bamboo the flute, the waterfall the drum, bees the lute, monkeys the audience and the peacock a dancer; Paripadal 21.30-38 has the peacock dance, the thumbi as flute, bees as lute and the waterfall as drum on the god's hill.
teaches: In the Akananuru the hill's orchestra is a love poem's setting, praising the hill man's country and ending in the woman's lonely night, while the Paripadal keeps the same instruments, drops the monkey audience and the lovers, and gives the scene to the god with the drum, so the pair shows a figure from akam landscape reused as worship of the hill's own god.

note: In Paripadal 6.88-92 a husband says a woman bathing in his pool, swept under by a wave, fell on him unbidden, and swears by cool Parankunram; in Paripadal 21.39-45 a wife at a pool on Parankunram loses her float and her husband plunges in and embraces her.
teaches: The Vaiyai song's husband uses a fall in the water as an alibi for touching another woman and swears by Parankunram, while the Parankunram song shows the water embrace on that hill as a husband's rescue of his own wife, so the pair shows one festival accident read either as an excuse for straying or as wedded love.

note: Paripadal 5.79-81 says what we ask of the god is not wealth, gold or pleasure (பொருளும் பொன்னும் போகமும் அல்ல) but grace, love and aram; Paripadal 21.68-70, after the drinking and dancing of the hill, asks that dwelling at his feet be granted as today (இன்று போல்), with their company.
teaches: The two Murugan songs end in prayers to the same god that pull apart: one refuses pleasure and asks for inner gifts, the other asks that a festival day of liquor, dance and couples simply recur, so the anthology holds both a moral and a festive idea of what worship should obtain.

note: Purananuru 107 answers the poets who praise Pari alone: there is also the rain (மாரியும் உண்டு) that sustains the world; Paripadal 22.8 says the sky poured water like the king's bounty (அவன் வண்மைபோல் வானம் பொழிந்த நீர்), after likening clouds, thunder, drops and lightning to his elephants, drum, arrows and spear.
teaches: Kapilar measures the patron against the rain and lets the rain win, while the Paripadal measures the rain against the king and makes the whole storm a copy of his war and gifts, so held together they show the rain-and-giving comparison run in both directions, with the river hymn making the king the original and nature the likeness.
audit_text_issue: Paripadal 22 lines 10, 12, 14, 15 have lacunae and line 13 is garbled.

note: Paripadal 8.112-117 says the eyes, faces, feet, hands, breasts and lips of girls rising from the hill pool cannot be told apart from the lotus and lilies of the water; Paripadal 22.32-34 says onlookers cannot decide whether the women adorn the Vaiyai or the Vaiyai's flood adorns them.
teaches: The hill song confuses women and flowers part by part, while the river song lifts the doubt to the whole, women against river, and refuses to settle which is the ornament, so the pair shows the Paripadal using the undecided likeness as its stock praise of festival bathing and widening it from a catalogue to a single question.

note: Paripadal 21.30-38 makes the peacock, thumbi, bees and waterfall into dancer, flute, lute and drum on the god's hill; Paripadal 22.36-44 has real drum, lute, flute and hand drum sounding with bees and thumbi at the Vaiyai ford, the wind as dancer (வளி நடன்), and says they exchange their work (தொழில் மாறு கொள்ளும்).
teaches: On the hill the orchestra is made of creatures only, while at the river the town's instruments and the grove's creatures play together and trade parts, so the two songs, set side by side in one chapter, show the hill as nature performing for its god and the ford as the town and nature performing with each other.

note: Purananuru 55.1-4 gives the mountain bow strung with a snake (பாம்புஞாண்) and the three forts burned with one arrow as the blue-throated god's feat, an emblem to measure the Pandya by; Paripadal Thirattu 1.80-82 says the serpent became the string of the Himalaya bow when the bull-rider destroyed the three cities and that it was they who gave him that ancient fame.
teaches: The same snake-strung bow is Shiva's glory in a court poem and the serpent's own merit in a shrine hymn, so the pair shows that a fixed myth could be re-credited to whichever power a cult served, the bowstring becoming the hero once it had a temple.

note: Paripadal 1.1-2 opens with the god's form whose thousand awful hooded heads (ஆயிரம் விரித்த அணங்குடை அருந் தலை) rise over his crown, white as a conch and carrying the plough; Paripadal Thirattu 1.83-85 uses the same words for a separate lord with his host, bowed to before the god is praised.
teaches: One formula line serves in the first song as a form of Mal himself and in this song as an attendant lord with his own retinue and his own deeds, so the anthology shows the serpent both absorbed into the god's body and kept as a distinct object of worship at his shrine.

note: Thiruppugazh 11 names Murugan's uncle as the one who sleeps on the serpent and who churned the sea of old (பனகம் துயில்கின்ற ... கடல் முன்பு கடைந்த); Paripadal Thirattu 1.68-75 gives the churning to the serpent, who lifted the mountain and was the rope while the discus-bearer (ஆழியான்) only pulled.
teaches: By Arunagirinathar's time the churning is simply Mal's act and the serpent his bed, while the Sangam hymn praises the rope for not breaking, so the pair shows the serpent losing its share of the myth as it became the god's couch.

note: Kural 1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one is sweeter than sleep in the soft arms of the one you love; Paripadal Thirattu 1.33-46 lists the shrine crowd as matched men and women and says the god's town is like the heaven where ripened deeds are enjoyed.
teaches: The couplet sets lovers' joy against Mal's heaven as rivals, but the hymn builds its likeness of heaven out of the paired lovers in the god's own crowd, so the opposition the Kural plays on was not one the temple festival felt.

note: Patitruppattu 31.1-10 shows crowds from the four quarters who go unfed (உண்ணாப் பைஞ்ஞிலம்), bathe at the cold ghat and praise the red feet of the tulasi-garlanded lord before going home glad; Paripadal Thirattu 1.43-46 shows the crowd at the god's town bearing food offerings, umbrellas, incense and flowers, in a town like a heaven of enjoyment.
teaches: Read together the two give two modes of early Mal worship, a fasting and bathing crowd in the Chera poem and a feasting, paired and pleasure-seeking crowd in the Koodal hymn, so devotion to the same god was already practised as abstinence in one place and as festival in another.

note: Kalittokai 98 has the husband excuse his absence by the Vaiyai's new flood (வையை வரு புனல் ஆடத் தவிர்ந்தேன்); Paripadal thirattu 2.36-39 has the rival excuse the lover's garland in her hair by the same flood (தானே புறன் தந்து வேய்தந்தது ... அறிந்து புனல் புணர்த்தது).
teaches: Held together, the two show that the festival flood was the stock excuse of the whole triangle: the man pleads it to his wife, and the other woman pleads it to the wife too, so the wife's scorn in the Kalittokai answers an alibi that every party in the Vaiyai festival could use.

note: Paripadal 6.44-51 has the learned brahmins dismayed that the flood is changed by flowers, roots, the food of common people and spilled toddy; thirattu 2.58-63 splits the refusal among பார்ப்பார், அந்தணர் and ஐயர, each for its own stain: toddy, lovers' wedding scents, honey.
teaches: The two songs together show that the priests' refusal to bathe was a set piece of the Vaiyai festival song, and the fragment's three causes make plain what song 6 only lists: every stain that bars the priest is a mark of the festival the town is enjoying, so the scene sets ritual purity against the river's festive use.

note: Akananuru 296 says the man's bathing in the great Vaiyai with the dark girl has become gossip in Koodal (அலர்ஆ கின்று, அது பலர்வாய்ப் பட்டே); thirattu 2.51-56 shows a woman wearing a garland from the flood openly, for the land to know (நாடு அறியப் பூ மாலை அப்பி), and the town's gossip following (ஊர்த்து அலர்).
teaches: The fragment shows how the gossip the Akananuru friend throws at the man was made: a love token worn in plain sight at the river festival, chosen by the woman as display, so the akam reproach of public shame rests on a festival custom in which the other woman wanted to be seen.

note: Paripadal 10.125-127 likens the flood pouring gold on the fields to the Vazhuthi pouring gold into poets' hands; thirattu 2.95-101 likens Maran bathing in the same flood with the people of Koodal to Indra bathing in the river of the sky.
teaches: Read together, the two Vaiyai songs place the Pandya on both sides of the flood: song 10 makes the river like the king in giving, the fragment makes the king like a god in bathing, so the king stands between the river's bounty below and Indra's heaven above, and the festival praises him through both.

note: Kural 118 likens the worthy man's impartiality to a balance that levels itself before it weighs; thirattu 7 has poets weigh the world against Koodal with the balance of their learning (புலக் கோலால் தூக்க).
teaches: Read beside the Kural's just balance, the fragment's praise borrows the authority of an impartial weighing, so the poets present their verdict on Koodal as fairness, the ornament of the worthy, rather than as a court singer's flattery.

note: Kalittokai 35 line 2 likens humming bees in the boughs to the enjoyment of those who live on a diligent man's wealth; thirattu 8 likens those who live on gifts (பரிசில் வாழ்நர்) to bees eating pollen.
teaches: The bee and the dependent were interchangeable figures that ran in both directions, a season described through patronage in Kalittokai and a society through a flower in the Paripadal, and only the Paripadal says whom the dependents feed on: the households, not the palace.

note: Kural 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except towering fame; thirattu 9 says Madurai's fame will stand and blossom as long as the king's hill exists (குன்றம் உண்டாகும் அளவு).
teaches: The Kural makes fame the one thing that does not perish, while the Paripadal blessing gives even the city's fame a term measured by a hill, so the poets' praise of undying renown was bounded by the oldest lasting things of the land.

note: Thirattu 9, 10 and 11 share one frame ('can Madurai decline ... as long as the king's ... exists'); 9 measures it by his hill, 10 by his Vaigai, 11 by his word (வார்த்தை).
teaches: Taken as a set, the fragments move the city's guarantee from a hill and a river to the king's word, so the last stanza rests Madurai's permanence on speech and renown, the poet's own stock, rather than on the land.

note: Purananuru 38 says bards think of Killivalavan's land even in the gods' golden grove, because there no one with means gives and no one in want asks (உடையோர் ஈதலும் இல்லோர் இரத்தலும்); thirattu 12 says Koodal honours givers and rejoices at receivers, so who would go to the gods' world (புத்தேள் உலகு)?
teaches: Purananuru 38 supplies the reason the fragment leaves unsaid, that heaven is poorer for lacking the exchange of giving and asking, so the Paripadal's preference for Koodal over heaven rests on an older argument first made for a king's land and here transferred to a city and its god's hill.

note: Kural 222 says taking is bad even if called the good path to heaven, and giving good even if there were no higher world; thirattu 12 praises a city that rejoices to see receivers (ஏற்பாரைப் பார்த்து உவக்கும்) and ranks its life above heaven. On the reading that ஏற்பார் are those who take gifts, the fragment honours the very taking the Kural calls bad.
teaches: Both cut the value of giving loose from heaven, but the Kural does it by condemning the receiver while the Paripadal makes the receiver's presence a joy of the city, so the two hold opposite views of whether asking belongs to the good life.

note: Kural 1014 asks whether shame (நாணுடைமை) is not an ornament of the worthy; thirattu 6 calls modesty the girl's ancient ornament (நாண் எனும் தொல்லை அணி) at her first union.
teaches: The same figure of shame as an ornament serves the Kural for the moral restraint of the worthy and the Paripadal for a bride's reserve at first union, which shows that naanam named both and that the poets ranked the bride's reserve above her jewels as the Kural ranks restraint above pride.

note: Kalittokai 35 counts Koodal's seasonal pleasures (bees on the Vaigai's sandbank, the festival, the townsmen savouring poets' new words) as the times the absent man promised to return; thirattu 13 lists the Vaigai flood, the god's hill and spear-eyed women as pleasures among which Koodal's people lose their way daily.
teaches: The same catalogue of Koodal's pleasures marks the hour of a promised return in the Kalittokai and causes daily indecision in the Paripadal, so the city's festive plenty was a stock that akam used to sharpen absence and city praise used to show abundance.
